10843-the-mental-life-of-monkeys-and-ape:
Robert M. Yerkes of Harvard published The Mental Life of Monkeys and Apes in 1916 as a Behavior Monograph edited by John B. Watson. The study tests three animals, Skirrl, Sobke, and Julius the orangutan, with multiple-choice problems and supplementary trials. Box stacking, box and pole, draw-in tests, and lock-and-key tasks measure their planning.

Yerkes asks whether apes and monkeys form ideas and solve problems by insight rather than habit alone. Six plates and five figures record the apparatus and results. Readers get a landmark of early animal psychology, careful in method and modest in its claims about animal minds.
11008-antwerp-to-gallipoli-a-year-of-the:
Arthur Ruhl, an American war correspondent, reported a year of the First World War from Antwerp to Gallipoli. Ruhl sailed from America on the St. Paul, crowded with reservists and correspondents, reached a Europe at war, and watched Paris at bay, the Marne, and the fall of Antwerp. Later chapters take him to German prison camps, trenches at La Bassee, and the road to Constantinople.

Ruhl visits Rumania and Bulgaria, follows the Turks at the Dardanelles, and reports from a correspondents' village, the Galician front, and the Russian retreat. Photographs illustrate the journey. The book reads as vivid firsthand reporting, curious about soldiers, civilians, and strange encounters, and it gives a broad view of the war's first year on many fronts.
11011-a-hilltop-on-the-marne-being-lette:
Mildred Aldrich wrote these letters from her house at Huiry, on a hilltop above the Marne, between June 3 and September 8, 1914. An American seeking a quiet refuge in France, Aldrich describes settling into country life, then watching war arrive: troops on the roads, carts carrying refugees.

Aldrich apologises in a later note for calling all British troops English, a colloquial error of the time. Her letters stay personal and observant, noting the cathedral tower at Meaux, neighbours' talk, and the strangeness of war seen from a garden. The book gives a civilian's view of the war's first summer, written day by day, before the front hardened.
11088-english-men-of-letters-crabbe:
Alfred Ainger wrote this 1903 life of George Crabbe for the English Men of Letters series. Ainger draws chiefly on the memoir by Crabbe's son, prefixed to the 1834 poems, with letters to Mary Leadbeater, manuscript sermons, and commonplace books lent by John Murray. Chapters follow Crabbe from Aldeburgh youth through London poverty and friendship with Burke.

Later chapters cover Belvoir Castle, Suffolk life, The Parish Register, The Borough, Tales, Tales of the Hall, and last years at Trowbridge. Ainger notes that Crabbe and Wordsworth, both weak self-critics, suffered in reputation from mixing good and bad verse. Walter Scott's 1809 letter, praising Crabbe after twenty years' admiration, shows the poet's standing among peers.
14058-readings-on-fascism-and-national-s:
Members of the University of Colorado philosophy department selected these readings on fascism and National Socialism, published by Alan Swallow in Denver. A prefatory note asks students to judge whether the readings form a coherent social philosophy, and whether those ideas are acceptable. Comparison with real and ideal alternatives is required.

Readings include Mussolini's Doctrine of Fascism and pieces on the movement's theory. One passage argues fascism, conceived qualitatively not quantitatively, is democracy in its purest form, a claim students are meant to test. The volume serves teaching, not advocacy. It suits courses on political philosophy and twentieth-century ideology. Its critical framing matters as much as its texts.
14191-as-we-are-and-as-we-may-be:
Bound with publisher lists for Besant and Rice novels, this volume of observation moves between London scenes and American history. One passage looks from a brewery window onto a hidden City churchyard, once full of tombs along a cloister walk, now cleared and bright with May flowers. A solitary officer of the brewery, master brewer or taster or chemist, enjoys the garden alone on summer evenings.

American chapters widen the view. Readers meet Lord Baltimore's tolerant Maryland, Carolina's lords proprietors and their aristocratic scheme, Quakers in Pennsylvania, and the temperance colony of Georgia. Germans arrive by thousands, and Irish Presbyterians flee a government that would force them into the Irish Episcopal Church. Persecution belonged to the times, the writer admits, yet calls this Irish misgovernment stupid beyond excuse. Social essay and history blend throughout.
15268-john-stuart-mill-his-life-and-work:
Twelve sketches by Herbert Spencer, Henry Fawcett, Frederic Harrison, and other distinguished authors honor John Stuart Mill, in a Boston volume of 1873. Fox Bourne sketches his life, Thornton his India House career, and Spencer his moral character. Botany, criticism, philosophy, morals, and political economy each get a sketch.

Fawcett treats his university influence and practical politics, while his wife Millicent writes on his political role. Harrison weighs positivism, and Hunter his place as a philosopher. The set offers a rich, contemporary portrait of Mill, written by friends and peers who knew his work.
1587-the-black-robe:
Wilkie Collins's The Black Robe opens before the story proper at Boulogne, where a duel leaves a legacy in dispute. A dying dowager, a Jesuit priest in a black robe, and a young heir caught between love and a religious order drive a plot of wills, conversions, and secret influence.

Collins, writing against Jesuit power as he saw it, builds his mystery from documents, confessions, and a trial of conscience. The tone is earnest and the plotting is intricate. The novel is a late Collins sensation tale, full of his old skill at turning a legal snare into drama.
1896-under-the-red-robe:
Stanley J. Weyman sets Under the Red Robe in the France of Cardinal Richelieu, whose red robe gives the book its title. The hero, a gentleman under sentence, is offered life in exchange for service: he must hunt down a rebel, and his honor must survive the bargain.

The chapters move from Zaton's inn to the Green Pillar and through a countryside of spies and swordsmen. A woman there sighs, rises, and notes that the afternoons are growing chilly before she goes in. Weyman writes the historical romance with polish. The novel's tension lies in a man serving a master he does not love for a cause he does not trust.
19448-talks-on-manures-a-series-of-famil:
Joseph Harris wrote this practical guide to manures and fertilizers as a set of talks between a farmer-author and his neighbors, the deacon, the doctor, and others. A new and enlarged edition adds a chapter by Sir John Bennet Lawes of Rothamsted, England, the famous farm research station.

Topics run from plowing clover under and killing weeds to raising larger crops per acre and judging wheat quality. The talk form keeps the advice homely: each claim is tested against field results. It remains a clear window on farming science before chemical fertilizers took full hold.
20064-captains-of-industry-or-men-of-bus:
James Parton published Captains of Industry in 1884, with the subtitle A Book for Young Americans. It tells the lives of business men who did something besides make money. Parton was a well-known life writer of his time. Here he turns to trade, craft, and public works.

One passage mocks rich men on Bellevue Avenue in fine carriages. Parton asks who truly counts for more, the showy rich or the useful worker. Each life in the book makes that case in a new field. Young readers were meant to learn drive, skill, and worth beyond wealth.
20847-india-what-can-it-teach-us-a-cours:
Max Muller owns, in his Cambridge lectures, that his host may not share his views. His bold dating of classical Sanskrit writing, he says, leaves him near alone. India: What Can It Teach Us still presses the case with warmth.

Muller, a great scholar of language, urges Britons to prize India's old books. The Vedas, laws, and tales of India fill his brief for respect. He taught that language study could bridge whole cultures. These lectures helped wake the West to Indian thought, even where later scholars revised his dates and claims.
22249-shorty-mccabe:
Sewell Ford introduced Shorty McCabe in 1906, and the ex-prizefighter became a magazine favourite. Shorty tells his own story in rich New York slang. There's a knockout coming to the best of them, he says, if they hang to the game long enough. He got his, clean and square, and he isn't ashamed of it or given to exhibiting himself on stage.

Retired from the ring, Shorty runs a gymnasium and solves other people's troubles. Ford lets him narrate swindles, romances, and fights in a voice all his own. The humour depends on the gap between Shorty's fists and his shrewd, kind heart. These stories were among the most popular magazine fiction of their decade.
23894-billie-bradley-at-three-towers-hal:
Janet D. Wheeler published Billie Bradley at Three Towers Hall in 1920, another volume in the Billie Bradley school stories. Billie, already known from her inheritance and her lighthouse island, now goes to boarding school, where the subtitle promises a needed rebellion.

Chapters bring almost a fortune, a wreck, and recovered treasure, then the Codfish, Amanda's surprises, and Miss Walters. At Three Towers Hall come the Dill Pickles, Lake Molata, lights out, and four enemies. Billie snores successfully, a plot fails, and Chet plays the hero. Raiding the pantry, a challenge, and a prisoner of war lead to a happy ending, with the girls sweeping down the school steps.
25208-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The September 1844 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 56, number 347, opens with an essay on Louis Blanc, the French democratic journalist writing a history of France since 1830. Blackwood's critics weigh his talents and his faults as a Parisian journalist turned historian.

Other pieces include a night on the banks of the Tennessee, the execution of Montrose, the first part of The Witchfinder, and a natural history of man. Poems by Coventry Patmore, another part of Marston's memoirs, and verses for the Burns festival round out a varied monthly number. The Burns verses, including stanzas signed Delta, honor Scotland's poet in festival mood.
26053-this-giddy-globe:
Peter Simple, fellow of the Terrestrial Globe, writes a comic geography in This Giddy Globe, edited and illustrated by Oliver Herford and printed by Doran in 1919. Dedicated to President Wilson, the book asks why the globe is giddy. It tours creation, a long jump, the equator, the earth's crust, temperature, age, face, climate, land and water, and the discovery of the world. Countries follow, from the poles and America to Boston, Canada, and Great Britain.

Herford jokes that Lief, after carving runes on a rock in America, sailed home to Norway, and his statue stands in Boston's Fenway to this day for his rudeness. Columbus, making four trips, carelessly wrote no book of impressions. The volume is light, learned fooling, with maps and pictures to match.
26487-little-lucy-s-wonderful-globe:
Charlotte M. Yonge narrates and L. Frolich pictures this children's geography, in a new edition of 1906. Little Lucy, allowed by Uncle Joe to touch a great globe, finds its peoples stepping out of the smoke to meet her. Mother Bunch welcomes her first, and visitors from the South Seas follow, tiny black figures who climb doors and chatter in the firelight.

Chapters then carry Lucy to Italy, Greenland, the Tyrol, Africa, Lapland, China, Kamchatka, and the lands of the Turk, Cossack, and Spaniard. In China a young hostess serves tea and remarks on Lucy's feet, while Paris in the siege and an American guest widen the tour. The book ends with a dream of all nations, teaching geography through wonder.
26528-odd-numbers-being-further-chronicl:
Sewell Ford's Odd Numbers, copyrighted from 1908 to 1912, continues the chronicles of Shorty McCabe, narrator of a physical culture studio, in his own slang. A highbrow regular proposes public information bureaus where strangers in New York might find friendly advice, from New Thought churches to fresh celluloid collars. Shorty answers with a shrug: Ain't I here?

Chapters follow Goliah and the purple lid, Maizie's coming through, Spotty, a grandmother who got going, and a long shot on DeLancey. Cornelia shows class, Marmaduke slips one over, Mrs. Truckles takes a broad jump, and Heiney tries the gloom cure. The stories mix sporting life, street wit, and soft-hearted rogues in Ford's breezy manner.
27507-the-giant-s-robe:
F. Anstey, author of Vice Versa, published this novel with Smith, Elder in London in 1884, in a third edition. Its epigraph comes from Macbeth: a title hangs loose about its wearer, as a giant's robe would on a dwarfish thief.

Anstey states in his preface that the central idea is a stolen manuscript. He credits a Christmas-number tale of a German student who found an old scientific manuscript in his university library, by a writer long dead and forgotten, and produced it as his own. That recollection, he says, became the unconscious germ of his book. The novel wears its borrowed robe with honest, independent work.
27609-the-undersea-tube:
L. Taylor Hansen wrote this science-fiction story, a classic reprint from Amazing Stories of November 1929, copyrighted by E. P. Incorporated. Its narrator claims he alone survived the much-discussed Undersea Tube disaster, reporting first to the International Committee for the Investigation of Disasters.

He bought a ticket on a fatal night only because his friend the engineer told him the Tube was dangerous. The story then sketches the tremendous difficulties of the engineers and the wind-propulsion theory behind the undertaking. By the close of the twentieth century, the long-heralded undersea railroad had at last been completed. The tale reveals the Golden Cavern and the City of the Dead.
28760-the-works-of-john-galsworthy-an-in:
David Widger edited this index to the Project Gutenberg editions of John Galsworthy's works. The index gathers the Forsyte Saga complete, with The Man of Property, Indian Summer of a Forsyte, Awakening, and To Let. It also lists Villa Rubein, Saint's Progress, Five Tales, The Island Pharisees, and novels like The Country House, Fraternity, and The Patrician.

Galsworthy's plays appear in six series, from The Silver Box, Joy, and Strife through Justice, The Skin Game, Loyalties, and Windows. His essays stand beside them. The index lets a reader move through a long career in order, novel by novel and play by play. It serves as a map to one of England's great chroniclers of family and class.
28970-works-of-george-w-peck-a-linked-in:
David Widger edited this linked index to the works of George W. Peck, author of the Bad Boy series. The index covers Peck's Bad Boy and His Pa in two volumes, Peck's Bad Boy Abroad, Peck's Uncle Ike and the Red Headed Boy, Peck's Sunshine, and Private George W. Peck. Detailed contents list every chapter and picture, from the boy with a lame back to Pa on the run.

Peck's humor comes from a boy's practical jokes on his Pa, told as newspaper sketches that became books. The index lets a reader find any joke, from a new way to take Seidlitz powders to Pa grabbed by the polonaise. It serves as a map to a once hugely popular American humorist, whose bad boy taught generations to laugh at family life.
2898-pioneers-of-the-old-south-a-chronic:
Mary Johnston wrote Pioneers of the Old South for the Chronicles of America series, tracing English colonial beginnings from the three ships that sailed after Elizabeth's death in 1603. James Stuart's accession opens the story, and chapters follow Jamestown, John Smith, the Sea Adventure, Sir Thomas Dale, and the growth of Virginia, Maryland, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Bacon's rebellion and the Navigation Laws close the arc.

Johnston quotes the colonists themselves, including Dale's warning that abandoning Virginia would be a blunder unmatched since the loss of France. The narrative keeps its focus on settlement, government, and conflict rather than legend. It gives readers a compact history of the southern colonies, written with a novelist's sense of scene.
29280-how-the-piano-came-to-be:
Ellye Howell Glover published this illustrated history of the piano in Chicago in 1913. Glover traces the instrument from sinews dried and stretched over a dead tortoise's shell to the modern piano. Along the way she shows the upright harpsichord, the clavichord, the spinet, Queen Elizabeth's virginal, and the dulcimer.

Key makers appear in the illustrations: Christofori, whose piano stands at a turning point, Stein, Crehore, Albrecht, and Stodart. Glover explains how hammers replaced plucking quills and gave players control of loud and soft. Readers get a clear, picture-filled history of a familiar instrument, useful for music lovers and for anyone curious how the piano earned its name.
30408-the-fifth-dimension-tube:
Murray Leinster tells The Fifth-Dimension Tube, a complete novelette from Astounding Stories, January 1933, and a sequel to The Fifth-Dimension Catapult. Tommy and Evelyn enter a hostile fifth-dimensional world of golden cities, tree-fern jungles, and Ragged Men through Professor Denham's tube. An illustration shows Evelyn swaying as the Thing moves. The tube chapter opens with a generator rumbling and roaring up to maximum speed.

The whole laboratory quivers from its vibration, the dynamo hums and whines, and night silence outside makes the noises within more deafening. Tommy Reames checks the power-leads to monstrous, misshapen coils, Professor Denham bends over one, straightens, and nods, and Evelyn throws the heavy multiple-pole switch. A flash of jumping current leaps, metal masses on the floor seem to leap into ungainly life, and the dynamo's whine rises to a scream with brushes streaking blue flame.
32026-the-world-that-couldn-t-be:
Clifford D. Simak's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1958, follows a farmer on an alien planet. Like every farmer on every planet, Duncan must hunt down anything that damages his crops. The story opens on his field. A raider has worked with method there. It sheared the vua plants an inch or two above the ground. It harvested the ten westernmost rows, then angled off into the bush.

The signs are fresh, with soil still trickling into deep pug marks sunk in fine loam. Around Duncan, a sawmill bird whirs through a log, chatterers click their morning song in thorn-choked ravines, and heat rises from desiccated dust under a newly risen sun. The tale's pull lies in that frontier routine made strange: a lone farmer, a damaged crop, and a creature that, by the story's title, should not exist at all.
38507-the-memoirs-of-charles-lewis-baron:
The third volume of the memoirs of Charles Lewis, Baron de Pollnitz, was printed at London in 1738 for Browne at the Black Swan and Brindley in New Bond Street. Pollnitz travelled from Prussia through Poland, Germany, Italy, France, Spain, Flanders, Holland, and England. His observations promise not only the present state of the cities and towns, but the characters of the persons at the several courts.

The translator's preface tells the book's odd history. The Amsterdam bookseller printed the work first in three volumes, then four, then five. The first three he called Letters; the last two, written earlier, are the Memoirs proper. Pollnitz had sold it at Paris, and it passed hand to hand before anyone compared it with the Letters and found it different. A soldier of fortune turned court gossip, Pollnitz sold Europe its drawing rooms, and the English reader of 1738 bought the translation.
38768-south-africa-and-the-transvaal-war:
Louis Creswicke wrote this history of the Transvaal War, printed at Edinburgh in 1900 in six volumes. The part held here is volume four, running from Lord Roberts's entry into the Free State to the battle of Karree. Maps and many plates fill the book, one showing the Queen hearing a dispatch from the front.

A dated table opens the volume. Chapters cover the vote of censure, Kimberley, and General French's ride of February 12 to 15. The herding and surrender of Cronje at Paardeberg take the heart of the book. Mafeking's siege months, Poplar Grove, Driefontein, and the entry into Bloemfontein on March 13 follow. The relief of Ladysmith closes the span, in a war still far from done.
39070-the-sun-changes-its-position-in-sp:
August Tischner wrote The Sun Changes Its Position in Space, printed at Leipzig in 1883, and dedicated it to all friends of rational astronomy. A Latin motto heads the title page. Tischner grants that the Copernican system is the only possible one, the base of all progress in the science.

His quarrel is with one part of it: the fixed sun. Science, he notes, now admits that the sun moves through space, yet keeps calling it at rest. Tischner calls that evasion a sophism and presses the point at length. He quotes Mädler in his support and Averroës against him. The tract is a footnote to nineteenth-century astronomy, argued with great heat.
42630-the-outdoor-chums-in-the-big-woods:
The Outdoor Chums in the Big Woods is a boys' novel by Quincy Allen, copyrighted in 1915. Its subtitle names the rival hunters of Lumber Run. The first chapter opens with a snowball battle. Four chums, Frank, Bluff, Jerry, and Will, face a larger enemy crowd. A well fired snowball knocks Bluff's hat clear off his head. Frank Langdon, the group's leader, accepts the dare.

Twenty five chapters carry the boys north to Maine. A broken window brings glorious news that starts the trip. Among the lumberjacks and in a lone cabin the hunt unfolds. Chapters promise game, fur and feathers, and a flashlight picture. A bear trap victim and a cook stampede add peril and fun. The big moose and the hour of triumph crown the hunt. A grey coated pirate from Canada closes the rivalry.
43423-old-mole-being-the-surprising-adve:
Old Mole holds the surprising adventures in England of Herbert Jocelyn Beenham, by Gilbert Cannan. Appleton printed it in New York and London in 1917, under a 1914 copyright. Cannan had written Round the Corner. He gives the book to his wife.

Beenham was sometime sixth form master at Thrigsby Grammar School in the county of Lancaster. Parts are named prelude, marriage, interlude, and toys. In the swim, out of it, and an appendix close the book. A sensitive observer, the text says, once spent a week in theatrical lodgings in Thrigsby. He described the moral air of the place as harsh listlessness shot with humor. It is farther than Beenham got in the twenty five years he gave to teaching the youth of Thrigsby. Novel fans get a quiet schoolmaster comic life.
44471-life-aboard-a-british-privateer-in:
Life Aboard a British Privateer in the Time of Queen Anne is the journal of Woodes Rogers. Chapman and Hall published the edition at London in 1889. Robert Leslie added notes and illustrations to the old sea journal. A plate shows the ship running past Minehead with a fine south east gale.

From King Road, Bristol, to Cork in Ireland opens the contents as chapter one. Amongst the Canary Islands and from Grande toward Juan Fernandez follow the route. From Lobos toward Guayaquil in Peru fills the fourth chapter of the voyage. Among the Galapagos islands and at Gorgona road comes next in the contents. Sailing toward Guam and Batavia, then round the Cape home, closes the journal. Rogers rescued Alexander Selkirk on that famous privateering voyage round the world.
4538-little-lucy-s-wonderful-globe:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this children's story around a sick girl, Lucy, who spends a strange fortnight in bed after breaking out in red spots. A wonderful globe becomes her way of travelling while she cannot leave the nursery. With Mother Bunch and a string of visitors, Lucy visits in turn the South Seas, Italy, Greenland, Tyrol, Africa, Lapland, China, Kamchatka, and many other lands.

Each chapter gives a short, vivid glimpse of a place: its people, clothes, work, and weather, told in simple language for young readers. Later stops include Switzerland, Spain, Germany, Paris during a siege, and an American guest, before a closing dream of all nations. Readers get a gentle geography lesson dressed as a sickroom fancy, warm, curious, and easy to read aloud.
45386-lincolniana-or-the-humors-of-uncle:
Andrew Adderup gathered Lincolniana, or the Humors of Uncle Abe, printed in 1864 at Springfield, Illinois. The book is a jest book of tales told of President Lincoln while the Civil War still raged. Adderup signs his preface on the first of April, a fit day for such a book.

An old joke, he says, is like painted glass in a kaleidoscope: each turn shows a new aspect that may be taken for the first. He claims only a godfathership for the little jokes, and asks every reader with a good thing to send it in for the complete edition. Uncle Abe, an involuntary Black Republican, is the hero of the tales: shrewd, droll, and hard to beat in a story trade.
46585-the-chronicles-of-crime-or-the-new:
The Chronicles of Crime, or The New Newgate Calendar, was edited by Camden Pelham of the Inner Temple. It gathers memoirs and anecdotes of notorious characters who outraged the laws of Britain down to 1841. The title page lists the stock. Coiners, forgers, fraudulent bankrupts, and footpads appear. Highwaymen, housebreakers, impostors, murderers, mutineers, pirates, pickpockets, and traitors follow. Fifty-two engravings from drawings by Phiz embellish the work.

Volume 1 opens alphabetically with cases such as Agnes Adams, forgery. The frontispiece shows the man with the carpet bag turned away from an inn. Pelham's collection, reprinted here in 1887, fed the Victorian appetite for criminal biography. It is a rogues' gallery in two volumes, half warning and half entertainment.
46595-the-chronicles-of-crime-or-the-new:
The Chronicles of Crime, or The New Newgate Calendar, volume two, is a rogue's gallery in prose. Camden Pelham, a barrister of the Inner Temple, wrote the memoirs. Miles printed the volume in London in 1891, with fifty-two engravings by Phiz.

The title page gives the scope: lives of notorious folk who broke the laws of Britain, from the earliest times to 1841. Coiners, forgers, footpads, and highwaymen head the roll. Housebreakers, impostors, murderers, mutineers, and pirates follow. Pickpockets, rioters, sharpers, and traitors round out the company. Some cases, the book boasts, had never been published before. The contents run by name, each with its charge: Brock for coining, Brandreth for treason. A gold dust robbery, piracy, coach robbery, and the Birmingham riots of 1839 all stand in it.
48156-california-as-it-is-and-as-it-may-:
F P Wierzbicki, a doctor living in San Francisco, wrote California As It Is and As It May Be in 1849. Its second title calls it a guide to the gold region. Washington Bartlett printed the first edition in San Francisco itself. The contents move from the country's resources to advice to the miner.

Wierzbicki had lived in California for years and crossed its whole extent. He spent more than four months in the gold region and crossed the Sierra Nevada to the desert's edge. His preface, dated September 30, 1849, claims his book fills a real want. Rival books had lately hurt California's name, he says. Chapters treat the towns and the harbor of San Francisco, with directions for entering the port. It is a gold rush guide written on the spot.
52896-life-and-travel-in-india-being-rec:
Anna Harriette Leonowens recalls a journey across India made in the years before railroads reshaped travel there. Her book was copyrighted in eighteen eighty-four. The copy shown here is the Philadelphia edition issued by Henry T. Coates and Company in eighteen ninety-seven, fronted by a view of the Taj Mahal from the river. Leonowens had already written about Siam, and she treats India as a place she lived in and watched closely.

Early chapters stay around Bombay, with hillside homes and the daily round of English households, then move to the island caves of Elephanta. Along the way she describes serpent charmers, street performers, and Parsee fire worship, with its priests, rites, and Tower of Silence. Later chapters head inland toward Poonah and Satarah, past hill temples and old palaces, recording dances, dramas, schools, and village life.
55387-one-hundred-proofs-that-the-earth-:
William Carpenter wrote One Hundred Proofs That the Earth Is Not a Globe, printed and published by the author at Baltimore in 1885 and sold for twenty five cents. Carpenter dedicated the book to Richard Proctor, whom he calls the greatest astronomer of the age. The book had reached its fifth edition and sixth thousand.

Carpenter lists his proofs one by one. Balloonists see no curve, standing water stays level, surveyors make no allowance, and rivers such as the Nile flow the wrong way for a globe. Lighthouses and a trip down Chesapeake Bay add their share. The book is a classic of flat earth writing, earnest in tone and sure of its case. It shows how a minority view argued its corner in print.
55437-historical-record-of-the-fifth-reg:
The Historical Record of the Fifth Regiment of Foot, or Northumberland Fusiliers, belongs to the official Historical Records of the British Army. A general order from Horse Guards, dated January 1, 1836, set the series going. The king commanded that an account of every regiment's services be published under the Adjutant-General.

The order fixed what each record must hold: the regiment's first raising, its stations, its battles and sieges, and the trophies it took. Names follow of officers and men killed or wounded, of those given titles or medals, and of men who stood out in action. Badges and devices borne on the colours are listed with the reasons they were granted. The preface says such records stir emulation and guard an army's credit. Regimental historians still mine these sober, detailed volumes for names, dates, and deeds.
59017-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 371, volume 60, was dated September 1846. Contents list a study of Mexico and its people, and a summer day poem by Thomas Aird. A piece on Cabrera, letters on English hexameters, an essay on Algeria, and a tale of the water cure follow. The number sold through all booksellers in the United Kingdom.

A long letter printed in the number comes from a London hotel in July 1846. Its writer protests an article called Rogues in Outline in the June issue, which had named him a rogue and a faker of antiques. He treats hints about his private life with contempt but vows to fight the charges on his trade honor. The letter shows the magazine's rough, personal style of debate.
59422-wisdom-s-daughter-the-life-and-lov:
Wisdom's Daughter: The Life and Love Story of She-Who-Must-be-Obeyed is a romance by Rider Haggard, printed at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1923. Haggard dedicates it to the memory of Andrew Lang. In bygone years She and Ayesha were dedicated to Lang; now, when he is dead, this last romance concerning She is offered as a tribute to his beloved and honoured memory. The dedication is dated from Ditchingham in 1922.

The frame is Haggard's familiar one. It contained two thick notebooks bound in parchment, of an extremely thin and tough paper not of European make. Sidon fills the middle: its king, Dagon's sacrifice, the vengeance of Beltis and the sea battle. The book is the prequel of She, written forty years on.
61155-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
Three Voyages of Captain Cook, volume three, is a sea narrative of exploration. Longman printed the seven volume set in London in the year 1821. This third volume opens the second voyage of Captain James Cook. A plate shows the landing at Middleburgh, one of the Friendly Isles. Maps and other plates enrich the complete set for readers then.

Contents resume the sequel of the search for a southern continent. That search ran between the Cape of Good Hope meridian and New Zealand. Cook's Resolution probed high southern latitudes for the fabled land mass. Ice fields, island peoples, and long ocean legs fill the ship's journal. The 1821 reader got the Admiralty voyages in a handy, cheap form.
61923-the-proportions-of-christian-liber:
The Proportions of Christian Liberality is a sermon in print from 1824. William Collyer spoke it to a meet of church chiefs and flocks. The meet sat at Trevor Chapel in Brompton on April 8, 1824. Its text is a line from Paul's note to the Galatians.

The line bids folk do good to all as they get the chance. It adds a first care for those of the house of faith. Collyer asks what share of one's means each claim should get. Claims on our funds grow fast, and no purse can meet them all. He asks how to sort true claims from weak ones with care. The doubt he starts with is the heart of the whole talk.
62659-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
The Three Voyages of Captain Cook holds the logs of a great sea chief. This book is the last of seven in the set, out in 1821. It is the third part of Cook's third and last trip on the seas. Captain King's log takes up the tale at this point of the set.

The scene is the bay where Cook met his death in the isles. Great crowds of the isle folk throng the shore in the first part. The chiefs hold great sway over the low folk of the isles there. A priest and war man pays a call on the ships at the start. The shrine of the bay, its rites, and the taboo are set out in full. The king of the isle lands in pomp and is met by Cook in turn. Theft and strife then stain the last days of the great chief.
63326-a-letter-of-affectionate-remonstra:
John Alexander, minister of Prince's Street Chapel in Norwich, protests a closed plan for infant schools in a letter issued in 1836. The pamphlet sold for fourpence and was dated at Norwich on March 28, 1836. Alexander signs his name, saying a signed protest is more respectful than an unsigned one.

A notice in the Norwich papers had called a meeting of members of the Established Church to spread infant schools in city and county. All other inhabitants were shut out, and the notice named neither its backers nor its chair. Alexander, one of the excluded, explains how Norwich infant schools had run on open lines so far. Readers get a sharp small pamphlet on church privilege, schooling for the poor, and fair dealing between Christians.
63642-ph-be:
Phœbe is a girls' novel by Eleanor Gates, copyrighted in 1919. Grosset and Dunlap published it at New York. Gates had written The Poor Little Rich Girl and Apron Strings. She dedicates the book to the little girl whose story it is. Phœbe is fourteen when a telegram changes her life. Her mother bids her pack a suit case and leave with her father for Grandma's.

The command startles the girl on the moving train. Her mother had left the New York apartment that morning with a gay kiss. Phœbe has never seen the grandmother she is sent to. Two uncles, a judge and a clergyman, are strangers to her too. She has always sensed that Mother dislikes them all. Why she is sent to them is the mystery that starts the tale.
64228-quest-on-phoebe:
James Adams wrote Quest on Phoebe, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1947. Ron Farr has come to Phoebe, a moon of Saturn, seeking the secret of eternal life. An elixir lies hidden there, guarded by jungle and by the devices of the ancients of the ringed planet. A dozen men went before him, and none of them returned.

Farr means to succeed where they failed. He lands away from the reputed region, since his instruments find a force-field above it that would crush a ship. Cliffs box the region in on three sides. The magazine's blurb shows him tearing through the jungle, snarling at the natives to keep their distance. Adams writes pulp adventure: one man, a death-guarded treasure, and a moon full of terrors between him and the power to master destiny.
6491-the-head-of-the-house-of-coombe:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Head of the House of Coombe begins many years ago. People then still believed in permanency and held singular confidence in the stability of possessions, desires, ambitions, and convictions. London, like other great capitals, felt itself final then. Before long the world, rocked to and fro, revealed in each pause a startling suggestion of new arrangement. Belief in permanency seemed lost, and inhabitants gazed helplessly at changing stars and colours.

Its opening incidents date from that earlier confidence, a time of ingenuousness and sometimes stupidity of type. A mid passage shows a tall, fair, wonderful person who was a Mother, before whom a child stands hand in hand with Donal like little worshippers before a deity. Andrews' sister has attired the small creature like a flower of spring, exquisite and physically brilliant. Burnett writes an old house, a child, and a world about to change.
66377-the-needed-change-in-the-age-of-co:
Richard Arthur, a doctor with degrees from both arts and medicine, wrote The Needed Change in the Age of Consent, printed at Sydney in 1896. Its subtitle calls it an appeal for the better protection of our girls, and Arthur writes with open anger at the law of New South Wales.

He states that a girl of fourteen years and a day could be ruined with no legal remedy unless brute force could be proved. Parliament, he charges, cared more for office and taxes than for shielding the weak. Rescue homes and hospitals, he says, were full of girls cast out by this license. His remedy is to raise the age of consent to at least eighteen, so the law guards girls through their most at-risk years. The pamphlet is a fierce piece of reform writing from colonial Australia.
68890-dogs-of-all-nations-a-complete-wor:
Dogs of All Nations is a full work on the breeds of the dog by W. E. Mason. It is rich in pictures and sets the kinds of dogs out by the lands they come from. With each kind goes matter that sets out its traits and its use. The work grew out of a show of live dogs at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition at San Francisco in 1915.

A note at the front tells patrons that great care was used in the gathering of the dogs in that show. Most of them, the note says, could be bought, with Mason as the man to write to. The author gives the book in thanks for the support his bid to gather all known breeds met with at that fair. A European office in Southport, England, is named on the title leaves as well.
70968-the-danube:
Walter Jerrold travels the Danube from source to sea in a pictured guide first issued in London in 1911. Thirty pictures by Louis Weirter back the text, twelve of them in color. Jerrold divides the river into four reaches, upper, Austrian, Hungarian, and lower.

The first chapter weighs two rival sources in the Black Forest, at St Georgen and at Donaueschingen. From there the route runs past Ratisbon, Passau, Linz, and the Wachau to Vienna. Budapest, Belgrade, and the Iron Gate follow, then Rustzuk and the run to the Black Sea. Castles, vineyards, gorges, and old towns crowd the banks in Jerrold's telling. Readers get a full Edwardian river journey, rich in history and scene.
72747-a-british-army-as-it-was-is-and-ou:
Lieutenant-Colonel James Campbell wrote A British Army As It Was, Is, and Ought to Be, published in London in 1840. Campbell had served as brigade-major of the third division in the Peninsular War, and in the 45th and 50th regiments. He dedicated the book to General Brisbane, under whom he had served. The Peninsula supplies his examples throughout.

Campbell's letter of dedication states his case plainly. British soldiers, he grants, will follow their officers in any attempt, and their courage is unmatched. But he is not blind to the great imperfections of too many men allowed to enter the regiments. His chapters observe India, America, Canada, the boundary line, the navy, and steam warfare. The book is a reformer's brief from inside the army.
a-hilltop-on-the-marne-being-letters-wri: Mildred Aldrich writes from a hilltop on the Marne in letters from June 3 to September 8, 1914. The letters follow the first weeks of war in France and the British expedition's arrival. Aldrich apologizes in a later note for calling all khaki troops English, as French usage then did. Her letters give a civilian's close view of war's opening.
antwerp-to-gallipoli-a-year-of-the-war-o: Arthur Ruhl reports a year of war from Antwerp to Gallipoli, on many fronts and behind them, as a correspondent watching the First World War. The chapters follow armies, aeroplanes, and civilians caught in the fighting. Ruhl's on-the-spot prose gives readers a vivid, ground-level view of the war's first year.
as-we-are-and-as-we-may-be:
Walter Besant gathered these essays on English life and institutions in a volume dated 1903. Besant, a London novelist who knew the city's charities and streets well, weighs how national wealth and old endowments actually serve the public. His title sets the pattern: first the thing as it stands, then the better shape it might take under honest reform.

One long case study audits the Royal Hospital of St Katherine near the Tower, where thousands of pounds a year support a barely wanted chapel. Besant sets waste against usefulness at roughly twelve to one, then faults an 1871 royal commission for letting the chance of reform slip. Figures, history, and plain indignation drive the argument toward secular, useful charity.
britannica-1911-arbe:
Arbe, or Rab, is an Adriatic island. It forms Dalmatia's northernmost point in Austria. The island is thirteen miles long. Its greatest breadth is five miles. Population in 1900 was 4,441. Its capital bears the same name. That town is walled and beautiful. It occupies a steep coastal ridge. A thirteenth-century cathedral crowns the promontory.

Four church belfries rise behind the cathedral. The castle stands behind them again. Desolate hills form the background. Many houses are roofless and untenanted now. Plague struck the town in 1456. It swept away most townsfolk then. Five centuries of prosperity ended abruptly. Some old palaces retain considerable interest. One was Marc Antonio de Dominis's birthplace. Fishing and agriculture sustain the islanders today. An ancient silk industry still survives.
britannica-1911-arcis-sur-aube:
Arcis sur Aube, a town of eastern France, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of a district in the department of Aube. It stands on the left bank of the Aube, north of Troyes on the rail line to Chalons. Its count in nineteen hundred and six was two thousand eight hundred and three.

Fires in three years in the seventeen and eighteen hundreds gutted the old town. What stands now is built in modern style, with wide and straight streets. A fine house of the old kind holds the site where Diana of Poitiers once lived. The church dates from the fifteenth century, and a statue of Danton, a son of the town, stands before it. Work in knit goods and trade in grain and coal fill out the portrait.
britannica-1911-aube:
Aube, a district of north east France, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Five districts bound it on its sides. It was formed in seventeen ninety from a part of Champagne and a small piece of Burgundy. Its area is two thousand three hundred and twenty six square miles. Its count in nineteen hundred and six was past two hundred and forty thousand.

The district lies in the Seine basin. The Seine and the Aube are its chief streams. Both follow the slope of the land from south east to north west. The top point stands in the south east at twelve hundred feet. The south and east parts are rich and well wooded. The rest is in the main a bare and dull plain with a famed poor name. The air is mild but damp.
britannica-1911-bar-sur-aube:
Bar sur Aube, a town of north eastern France, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of an arrondissement in the department of Aube, 34 miles east of Troyes. It lies on the main line of the Eastern railway between Troyes and Belfort. Its count in 1906 was 4,276 souls in the town.

The town sits at the foot of hills on the right bank of the Aube, where the Bresse joins it. A ring of boulevards marks the line of its old ramparts, parts of which still stand. Two churches of the late 1100s are picked out for note. Saint Pierre has wooden galleries outside and two fine Gothic porches, while Saint Maclou may hold the chapel of the old castle in its sacristy. Trades are flour milling, tanning, brandy, hosiery, and farm tools, and the wine of the district is much esteemed.
britannica-1911-bari-tribe:
The Bari are a Nilotic people living on the banks of the upper Nile, some 200 miles north of Lake Albert. Their neighbours are the Dinka to the north, the Madi to the south, and the Galla to the east. The 1911 Britannica entry describes their dress, with married women wearing a red-dyed goatskin, and their use of red clay as body ornament.

Cattle are their sole wealth, and milk and blood their chief food; meat is eaten only when a cow happens to die. They live in round grass huts with conical roofs. Rainmakers rank as the most important men in the country, revered even above the chiefs. The entry closes by noting Bari recruitment into the Egyptian army.
britannica-1911-barnes-barnabe:
Barnabe Barnes (about 1569–1609) was an English poet, fourth son of Dr Richard Barnes, bishop of Durham, born in Yorkshire. He entered Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1586, where Giovanni Florio served under him, and in 1591 he went to France with the earl of Essex, then campaigning against the prince of Parma.

On his return Barnes printed Parthenophil and Parthenophe, a book of sonnets, madrigals, elegies, and odes, entered on the register in 1593 and dedicated to his friend William Percy. It may have been printed for private circulation, and the copy in the duke of Devonshire's library is thought unique. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his deep debt to the French sonneteers of his day and the faint story that can be traced through his love lyrics.
britannica-1911-beja-tribe:
Beja is the name of a wide family of tribes, classed as a rule as Hamitic. They may in fact stand for very early Semitic settlers in their land. When first put on record, the Beja held the whole region between the Nile and the Red Sea. That stretch runs from the border of Upper Egypt to the foot of the Abyssinian plateau. The old Egyptians knew them and carved their forms on stone.

The Beja are the Blemmyes of Strabo. Some take them to be the Macrobii of Herodotus, whom he called the tallest and finest of men. In the Roman age the Beja were much what they are now: folk who roam with their herds and press hard on their neighbours. They were at war again and again in those years. In AD 832 the Muslim governor of Assuan made a treaty with them.
britannica-1911-carpi-tribe:
Carpi is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Dacian tribe settled on the lower Danube from the first century B.C. The tribe rose to real power during the third century A.D. Holding themselves above the Goths, they demanded that Rome buy off their raids with tribute, as it did for others. When Rome refused payment, they invaded in force.

The emperor Philip beat them back, and they then joined the Goths in raids that met defeat under Claudius Gothicus. After further losses under Diocletian and Galerius, Rome took them under its protection. Most of the tribe was settled inside the empire, in Pannonia and Moesia, though some stayed beyond the Danube. They last appear as allies of the Huns and Sciri in the time of Theodosius I. The entry also notes Ptolemy's Harpii and the town Harpis as forms of their name among Germanic neighbours.
britannica-1911-cazembe:
Cazembe is the birth name passed down of an African chief whose land lay south of one great lake and north of an other. At the close of the seventeen hundreds his sway was owned over a very wide district. His kingdom bore his name as well.

The realm held on, the 1911 Britannica entry says, though its power and span shrank by slow steps. By the last part of the next age its chief had sunk to the rank of a petty lord. The land is now split between a British colony and the Belgian Congo, and its chief town in the British half bears his name. Its folk, who had beat the first tribes of the land, tilled with care and made cloth, clay ware, and iron goods. Rich copper lay in its soil.
britannica-1911-combe: Combe, also spelled coomb, is a term used most in south west England for a short closed valley. A brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry explains the word. Such a valley may sit on the side of a down or run up from the sea. It shows in place names as an ending, as in Ilfracombe, and as a start, as in Combemartin. The root is obscure, but hollow seems a shared sense.
britannica-1911-glebe:
Glebe is a church law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the land set aside to support a parish priest. The word comes from a Latin term for a clod of earth, and so for soil or land. In church law the glebe is the land given to keep the man who holds a church.

The article quotes Burn: by common right every church is entitled to a house and glebe. In old canon law the house and glebe went together under the name manse. One whole manse, free of all service, was to be given to each church. In the technical speech of English law, the ownership of the glebe is said to be in abeyance. The freehold rests in the parson, yet at common law he could sell it only with due consent.
britannica-1911-jaubert-pierre-amedee-em:
Pierre Jaubert is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a French scholar of the East from 1779 to 1847. He was born at Aix in Provence in June 1779. He was a star pupil of a famed teacher of tongues. He served as translator for Napoleon in Egypt. On his return he held state posts in Paris.

Trips east took him to Constantinople and to Persia. On the Persia trip he was seized and held in a dry pit. Four months passed before his captor died and freed him. He still made the pact with the shah he was sent to win. In 1818 he brought four hundred Kashmir goats to France. Later years went to study, writing, and teaching posts. He taught Persian and led a school of eastern tongues.
britannica-1911-jube:
Jubé is the French term, taken from a Latin command word, for the chancel or choir screen known in England as the rood-screen. Above the screen ran a gallery or loft. From that loft the deacon spoke the words Jube Domine benedicere before the reading of the Gospel, and the screen most likely took its name from that custom.

One of the finest screens in France is that of the church of the Madeleine at Troyes, built in rich flamboyant Gothic. A later one, of about 1600 and in the Renaissance manner, stands in the church of St Étienne du Mont in Paris. The Low Countries hold many fine examples in marble. One of the most perfect, brought from Bois-le-Duc, is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. The entry is short: a term, its likely origin, and a guide to the best screens to see.
britannica-1911-jujube:
Jujube is the name used for the fruits of at least two species of Zizyphus, Z. vulgaris and Z. Jujuba. The fruits feed and soothe, and a broth made from them was once advised for chest complaints. A thick paste of gum arabic and sugar, worked in a broth of the fruit, was also sold as jujube paste.

Z. Jujuba is a tree of 30 to 50 feet, found wild and planted in China, the Malay islands, Ceylon, India, tropical Africa, and Australia. The Chinese grow many kinds, told apart by the shape and size of the fruit, prized as a dessert and at times shipped to England. As sold, a jujube is about the size of a small filbert, with a red brown, shining, creased skin. Inside sits a yellow pulp round a hard, long stone.
britannica-1911-la-grand-combe: La Grand' Combe is a town of southern France, in the department of Gard, standing on the Gardon, 39 m. N.N.W. of Nîmes by rail. In 1906 the town held 6406 people and the commune 11,292. Extensive coal mines lie in the country round it, and the coal gives the place its work.
britannica-1911-macabebe:
Macabebe is a town of the province of Pampanga, on the island of Luzon in the Philippine Islands, as the 1911 Britannica entry gives it. It stands on the Pampanga Grande river, some ten miles above its mouth and twenty-five miles north-west of Manila. Its count in 1903, after the town of San Miguel was joined to it, was 21,481.

The tongue of the place is Pampango. Many of its men serve in the army of the United States as scouts. Its chief trades are the growth of rice and sugar cane. Men there distil spirits from the nipa palm, and weave cloth of hemp and cotton.
britannica-1911-morecambe: Morecambe is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Lancashire seaside town. It stands on Morecambe Bay, 236 miles from London, and is served by two railways. Its population in 1901 was 11,798. A fine promenade runs along the shore, with a quay and a pier, a winter garden, and all the fittings of a seaside resort. The Midland railway is the harbour authority. The town was incorporated in 1902, and its earlier name was Poulton-le-Sands.
britannica-1911-niobe:
Niobe, a figure in Greek myth, is explained in a legend entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, king of Thebes. Proud of her six daughters and six sons, she boasted over her friend Leto. Leto had only two children, Apollo and Artemis.

In punishment Apollo slew her sons and Artemis slew her daughters. The bodies lay unburied for nine days, since Zeus had turned the people to stone. On the tenth day the gods buried them in pity. The gods then turned Niobe herself into a rock on Mount Sipylus. In that form she wept without end. The entry sorts the cliff that bore her name from an older carved figure nearby. Views that read her as a goddess of snow or of earth are also weighed.
britannica-1911-nossi-be:
Nossi-bé, an island off the north-west coast of Madagascar, is given a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. Its name means Great Island. It runs 14 miles long by 10 broad, on 130 square miles. The island is volcanic, with old cones north and south and newer ground in the middle. Its high point, Lokobé, stands 1,486 feet above the sea.

Crater lakes dot the island. The count in 1902 was 9,291 people, and Hellville, the chief town, is a port of call. The soil is rich, and chief products are coffee, sugar cane, cocoa, and vanilla, with rum stills. The French took the island in 1841, and in 1896 it passed under the rule of Madagascar.
britannica-1911-oneida-tribe:
Oneida is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a tribe of North American Indians. The name is a corruption of their proper name, Oneyotka-ono. That name means people of the stone in their tongue. It alludes to the Oneida stone, a granite boulder held sacred. The tribe is of Iroquoian stock. It formed one of the Six Nations of the League. They lived around Oneida Lake in New York state.

Their land ran southward to the Susquehanna river. They were not loyal to the League's policy toward the English. They inclined toward the French in that long rivalry. They were practically the only Iroquois to fight for the Americans. As a result, other Iroquois under Joseph Brant attacked them. They took refuge within the American settlements till war ended. Some migrated to the Thames river district in Ontario.
britannica-1911-pont-l-abbe:
Pont-l'Abbe is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pont-l'Abbe is a town in western France, in the Finistere district southwest of Quimper. It stands on the right bank of its river, two miles from the sea. By 1906 the commune had over six thousand people. Its port fishes and trades in timber, coal, grain, and vegetables.

The article notes a church from the thirteen and fourteen hundreds, once tied to a Carmelite house. An old castle now holds the town hall. The town is famed for bright embroidery on local dress. The women's head dress is so marked that its name is given to the people themselves. Town trades include flour milling. Another trade takes chemicals from seaweed gathered on the coast.
britannica-1911-renaudot-eusebe:
Eusebe Renaudot, who lived from 1646 to 1720, was a French church scholar. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his late blooming fame. He was born in Paris and trained for the church. Most of his life, though, passed at the French court.

Colbert marked Renaudot out for trust work in state affairs. Deep learning in Eastern tongues grew through those court years. It bore no fruit in print until he was sixty-two. His best known book tells the patriarchs of Alexandria. A second great work gathers the liturgies of the East. Both aimed to prove the faith had stayed one through time. That claim sat at the heart of French church debate then. Fairness in dispute was not his strength, the entry admits.
britannica-1911-rich-barnabe:
Barnabe Rich is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English writer and soldier born near fifteen forty. Kin to a lord chancellor, he fought in the Low Countries and rose to captain. He later served in Ireland and helped plant new towns in Ulster.

The entry notes the pamphlets and tales he wrote between his wars. His best known book bids farewell to the soldier trade in its title. Eight tales fill that book, some forged for fun and some from Italian sources. One tale in it gave the Bard a plot for a famed stage comedy. Late honours mark him as the oldest captain still in service.
britannica-1911-tube:
Tube, a pipe or hollow round bar, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. Tubes carry fluids and gases in works of all kinds. They are made of many stuffs and sizes to suit each task, with metal pipes the most weighty. Metal tubes split into two kinds by the way they are made, seamed and seamless.

One early use of seamed iron tubes was for gun barrels, made by welding lapped strip edges. Gas light spread the need for tubes in homes and towns. In 1824 James Russell brought in the butt welded tube, with edges that meet but do not lap. A year later a new way drew the bent strip through a die. Seamless tubes, made by drawing pierced metal, are the stronger kind.
britannica-1911-wardrobe:
Wardrobe is the name of an upright cupboard for storing clothes. The 1911 Britannica entry traces its growth from the plain chest of old. For long the chest was the sole store for dress in homes. True closets came only when great palaces and castles gained rich garb. Then the name wardrobe fell to a room lined with cupboards and lockers.

The drawer is a late device in that tale of storage, it notes. From those rooms the modern wardrobe grew by slow steps in craft. It gained hanging space, sliding shelves, and drawers in due time. As a movable oak hanging cupboard it dates to the early 1600s. Such pieces were vast and heavy, with oft carved fronts of skill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbe: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbé explains a French word meaning strictly, the head of a men's monastery. From the reign of Francis the First, who named secular clerics as commendatory abbots with the Holy See's consent, the word widened to cover any man in secular clerical dress. In later centuries it was given to clerics who often held no holy orders, working as professors or tutors in noble houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-derbe:
A place entry on Derbe, a titular see of Lycaonia in Asia Minor. Once a bandit chief's fortress, it fell to Amyntas, last king of Galatia, and later struck its own coins under Rome. Paul and Barnabas evangelized it, Paul returned on a later journey, and it became a suffragan see of Iconium.

Only four bishops are known, spanning 381 to 672, and later bishop lists drop the see entirely. Its site stays unproven, argued from Strabo and Dio Cassius across rival guesses from Bin Bir Kilissé to Güdelissin near Konia, the last judged most likely. Readers chasing the debate get the older travel and survey works that weighed each candidate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-mccabe:
Edward McCabe was Cardinal Archbishop of Dublin in the troubled Land League years, born in Dublin in 1816 and dead at Kingstown in 1885. Son of poor parents, he was schooled on the Dublin quays and at Maynooth and ordained in 1839. After curacies at Clontarf and the Dublin pro-cathedral he turned down the see of Grahamstown in South Africa, preferring parish work at home.

He served Saint Nicholas Without from 1856 and Kingstown from 1865, becoming vicar-general. Cardinal Cullen chose him as assistant in 1877, and McCabe became Archbishop of Dublin in 1879 and cardinal in 1882. In pastorals and speeches he opposed agrarian agitation and sided with law and government, which won him the hostile label of Castle bishop from Nationalist papers and speakers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-malh:
Francois Malherbe, born at Caen in Normandy in 1555 and dead at Paris on 16 October 1628, was a French poet who disciplined the French language for the classical age. Eldest son of Francois Malherbe, councillor of Caen's lower court, and Louise de Valois, he was meant for his father's legal office and studied at Caen, Paris, Basle, and Heidelberg.

 After his patron was killed in a duel in 1586 he returned to Caen and addressed an ode to Henry IV on Marseilles in 1596. In 1600 he presented verses to Maria de' Medici at Aachen that show his talent mature. Du Perron recommended him to the king, and in 1605 he came to Paris, where his clear, correct verse and severe criticism of looseness shaped French poetry for a century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glebe:
Glebe, from the Latin gleba, originally meant any farm, estate, or parcel of land in common law, and is so used in the Theodosian Code. In ecclesiastical law it became the technical term for land permanently assigned to maintain the incumbent of a parish, the oldest form of parochial endowment. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a word that once barred consecration without endowment.

Formerly no church could be consecrated unless endowed with a house and glebe. The fee-simple was held in abeyance, without an owner in law. The freehold belonged to the incumbent, who could lease, sell, or exchange it with the bishop's consent. In the Catholic Church glebe counts as mensal property, and its alienation now generally needs the pope's special permission. That permission covers only necessity, utility, ransom of captives or feeding the poor in famine, or convenience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hautecombe:
Savoy's Cistercian abbey of Hautecombe, near Aix-les-Bains on Lake Bourget, was founded about 1101 by hermits from Aulps. It moved in 1125 to a shore site given by Amadeus, Count of Savoy, soon taking the Cistercian rule from Clairvaux. Its first abbot, Amadeus de Haute-Rive, later became Bishop of Lausanne, and daughter houses reached Italy and Constantinople.

Its chief fame is as burial place of Savoy's counts and dukes, from Blessed Humbert III in the twelfth century to Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, buried in the sanctuary. The last abbot, Anthony of Savoy, was buried there in 1673. Secularized in 1792 and turned into a china factory, it was bought back by Charles Felix of Sardinia in 1824, rebuilt, and restored to the Cistercians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jewish-tribe:
Jewish Tribe examines the Hebrew words shebet and matteh, both rendered tribe, each meaning branch, rod, staff, or sceptre. The figure likely points to a tribe as a branch of Jacob's family. It may also mean a company led by a chief bearing staff or sceptre, an order natural to Semitic nomads like today's Bedouin. .

Twelve tribes stand at the heart of Old Testament records and recur in the New, yet scholars dispute their origin. If patriarchal history is personal, each tribe descends from a son or grandson of Jacob: six by Leah, two by her maid Zilpah counted as Leah's. Two came by Rachel, and two by Rachel's maid Bilhah, Joseph alone giving his name through Ephraim and Manasseh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-deharb:
Joseph Deharbe was a German Jesuit whose catechism taught generations of Catholics. Born at Strasbourg in Alsace in 1800, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1817, taught at Brieg in Switzerland, and worked as a missionary and catechist at Cöthen. Feeling the lack of a sound catechism, he was ordered by his superior to write one himself.

His Katholischer Katechismus of 1847 won swift approval and was adopted diocese by diocese across Germany, then in Switzerland, Austria-Hungary, and the United States. Translated into many tongues, from Magyar and Polish to Marathi and Danish, it stayed in use in most German dioceses and in schools abroad well into the twentieth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-aleg:
Philippe Alegambe was a Belgian Jesuit historiographer, born at Brussels in 1592. After his studies he served the Duke of Osuna in Spain and followed him to Sicily, where he entered the Society at Palermo in 1613. He studied at Rome, taught philosophy and theology at Graz, and travelled Europe for years as preceptor to the Prince of Eggenberg. His last years passed at Rome as superior of the Jesuit house and secretary to the general.

His fame rests on the Bibliotheca Scriptorum Societatis Jesu of 1642, a continuation and enlargement of Ribadeneira's catalogue of Jesuit writers, carried to 1608. He also wrote Heroes and Victims of Jesuit Charity, a life of Father João Cardim, and acts of St. Justa drawn from manuscripts. The bibliography he built became the standard guide to the Society's authors. He died at Rome in 1652.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phillipe-l-ab:
Philippe Labbe was a French Jesuit scholar of history, geography, and philology, born at Bourges in 1607. He entered the Society in 1623, taught rhetoric, philosophy, and theology for five years in the last chair, and earned a reputation for quick memory and vast, accurate learning. With Petau he ranked as the most remarkable of French Jesuits in history, producing a work or more every year.

After his death his notes on all kinds of authors were found to exceed in bulk what an ordinary scholar reads in a lifetime. He had also spent much time answering others' questions on history, literature, and theology. Sommervogel lists over eighty of his works, from a Greek primer that ran through thirteen editions to his Royal Geography. He also wrote elegant Latin verse to Christ and Mary. He died at Paris's College of Clermont in 1667.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-webbe:
Samuel Webbe, English composer, was born in 1742 and died in London on 29 May 1816. Trained under Barbaudt, he won a Catch Club prize medal in 1766 for O that I had wings. In all he took twenty-seven medals for canons, catches, and glees, among them Discord, dire sister and Glory be to the Father. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs a popular musician of the Catholic chapels.

In 1776 he succeeded George Paxton as organist of the Sardinian embassy chapel, holding the post until 1795, and he also played at the Portuguese chapel. His Collection of Motetts of 1792 and his Collection of Masses for Small Choirs served Catholic churches across Britain for decades. Devotional if not of the highest order, some pieces are still sung. Nine books of glees between 1764 and 1798 remain his best claim to fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-segorbe:
Segorbe, a Spanish diocese taking in parts of Castellón, Valencia, Teruel, and Cuenca and suffragan to Valencia, is traced here from its ancient roots to the early modern period. The town is commonly identified with the Segobriga of Pliny, capital of Celtiberia. That suggests a bishopric of great age. Yet no bishop's name survives before Proculus, who signed at the Third Council of Toledo.

A run of early bishops who signed at the councils of Toledo carries the story to the Arab invasion. At that point the church became a mosque. The entry then follows the see's revival, with a bishop set up at Albarracín in 1172 after its capture by Pedro Ruiz de Azagra. It closes with the diocese's later shape and sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ailbe:
St. Ailbe was bishop of Emly in Munster, dying about 527 or 541, and this entry is frank about how little solid history survives beneath the legends. Beyond the disputed fact that he was a disciple of St. Patrick and probably ordained priest by him, almost nothing certain is known, and the Acts that picture him preaching before Patrick are quite untrustworthy.

Legend tells how the infant Ailbe, left in the forest for wolves, was suckled by a she-wolf. And how years later, as bishop, he sheltered that same wolf from hunters and fed her and her cubs daily in his hall. The entry retells the charming tale while marking it as legend, a model of how hagiography and history must be kept distinct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unyanyembe:
Unyanyembe was a vicariate apostolic in German East Africa, cut off from the Vicariate of Nyanza by a decree of Propaganda on 30 December 1886. Its limits, fixed on 10 December 1895, ran from Southern Nyanza in the north to a line drawn from Lake Manjara along mountain ridges in the south. Lake Tanganyika and the Congo Free State bounded it in the west. The district had first belonged to the Vicariate of Tanganyika.

In 1879 Father Ganachan of the White Fathers pushed into this unknown region and tried to settle at Tabora, without success. Two years later Father Guillet succeeded and opened an orphanage there, later moved to Kipalapala. The entry lists the vicariate's stations, priests, and peoples, giving a compact administrative portrait of a young mission field in the African interior.
doe-osti-17013568-fy25-updates-to-the-nr:
Idaho and Argonne national laboratories jointly updated a computer model of the DOME test site shield in fiscal year 2025. Lise Charlot and colleagues from both labs wrote the report, dated September 2025. DOME is a test site for microreactors, and its virtual twin sits in the National Reactor Innovation Center online test bed for vendors.

Updates automated a two step workflow, split between core and shield math, using Python scripts. The workflow was applied to a gas cooled microreactor design and produced dose rate maps for neutrons and photons. A linked heat model lowered the estimated concrete temperature of the shield. Photon dose spread still needs more work, the authors note.
doe-osti-2572081-strong-motion-dynamics-:
A research report by Marc Berghouse and Rishi Parashar studies how swimming bacteria move through the pore spaces of soil and sediment, and what that motion does to chemical reactions underground. The setting that matters most is the hyporheic zone, where surface water and groundwater mix. Work there supports cleaning up contaminated groundwater and protecting water quality.

Experiments showed that flow speed reshapes where microbes gather. At higher flow rates, swimming gives way to drift, and species with many flagella, such as Paenibacillus, keep their motility better than single-flagellum species. Against earlier assumptions, motile bacteria gathered in medium-speed regions, not only in slow pockets. Two tools came out of the work. DeepTrackStat reads motion statistics from microscope videos with less computing than older trackers. STAMNet, a neural network, carries the small-scale behavior up into fast large-scale predictions.
doe-osti-3012505-quantifying-and-optimiz:
Oak Ridge final CRADA report ORNL/TM-2025/4064, by Mikael Salonvaara, Andre Desjarlais, Niraj Kunwar, and Robert Pickett, measures the energy behavior of mass timber construction. The work was done with the International Mass Timber Alliance under CRADA NFE-21-08867. Test cubes built from cross-laminated timber, called CLT, were compared with lightweight-frame cubes in lab chambers and in field tests across three climates.

Under matched temperature settings, the CLT cubes used more total heating and cooling energy than the frame cubes. The gap, though, ran only 35 to 60 percent higher, well under the 100 percent extra that insulation values alone predicted. Peak heating and cooling demands were often about equal, since the heavy timber stores heat and softens peaks. The findings help builders judge where mass timber's thermal mass pays off.
doe-osti-3363631-assessment-of-bpm-optio:
Victor Smaluk of Brookhaven National Laboratory assesses beam position monitor options for the Electron-Ion Collider's Beam Accumulator Ring. The report is BNL-229706-2026-TECH, dated April 2026. The ring sits in the injection chain. That chain delivers polarized electrons for studying proton and nuclear structure. The monitors track beam position inside two candidate vacuum chambers.

One design reuses the NSLS VUV monitor in a rectangular chamber. The chamber measures 80 by 40 millimeters. The other design uses an octagonal chamber. Its shape accepts reused MIT Bates quadrupoles, which saves cost. Smaluk computes button electrode signals for both designs. He also computes capacitance and sensitivity. His test case is a 1 nanocoulomb bunch after the first injection. That is the worst case, when the beam signal is smallest.
doe-osti-3365790-exploring-the-feasibili:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21501, by Jessica Nguyen, Joshua Romano, David Barton Smith, and Michael C. Devin, explores whether fiber-optic sensing can watch over offshore mooring lines. Mooring lines hold floating marine energy devices in place, and a failing synthetic line is expensive and dangerous. Embedding optical fibers could turn the whole line into a strain sensor.

The team evaluated fiber materials, interrogation methods, and rope embedment approaches for distributed strain measurement. One thread works through ultraviolet processing of CYTOP fiber. Reaching the needed exposure would take about three hours at the assumed rate. The resulting index change is too poorly characterized to predict reflections directly. The feasibility verdict therefore rests on closing such characterization gaps. Findings guide designers of instrumented moorings for wave and tidal energy systems.
doe-osti-3366756-nondestructive-evaluati:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory letter report TLR-RES/DE/MEB-2026-01, by Muthu Elen, Nick Conway, Matt Prowant, and Richard Jacob, evaluates nondestructive examination of carbon fiber reinforced polymers for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Composite wraps and components are entering nuclear service, and inspectors need methods that find damage without cutting parts open. The April 2026 report documents mockup-based trials.

Mockups were built on steel substrates with deliberate flaws. For two of them, one quadrant was left unsandblasted before priming. That let inspectors test whether examination methods catch the effects of improper surface preparation. Primer and composite layup followed design requirements, with photographs in an appendix. The work gives the regulator evidence on what current nondestructive methods can and cannot see in composite repairs.
doe-osti-3377888-africa-battery-energy-s:
Paul Gasper of the National Laboratory of the Rockies teaches lithium-ion battery degradation and performance in an April 2026 slide deck for an Africa battery storage capacity building program. The deck was produced while the laboratory operated as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. It opens with battery basics: common positive electrodes are NMC and LFP chemistries, the negative electrode is almost always graphite, and the electrolyte is LiPF6 in a carbonate liquid.

Practical guidance follows. Keep battery temperature below 40 degrees Celsius, noting that a vehicle parked in the sun can reach that point when the air is only 30 degrees. Most chemistries should avoid deep discharge, though LFP tolerates it. Later sections compare degradation models and data sheet lifetimes against real-world system problems.
doe-osti-3378273-africa-battery-energy-s:
Five National Laboratory of the Rockies staff, Barbara O'Neill, Rebekah Townsend, Juliana Williams, Natasha Musalem, and Mike Campton, teach utility-scale storage valuation in an April 2026 Africa capacity building deck. The subject is how a large battery gets valued, tariffed, and paid, in that order. A five-step overview frames the session: policy and legal framework, cost breakdown analysis, benchmarking and validation, financial sensitivity and risk analysis, and public interest review.

The cost breakdown separates capital spending, battery modules, inverters, balance of system, civil works, interconnection, and land, from operating costs such as maintenance, staffing, insurance, and degradation replacement. Financing costs and revenue assumptions complete the picture. Two laboratory tools support the modeling: the System Advisor Model for costs and performance, and the Annual Technology Baseline for capital cost comparisons.
doe-osti-3818342-understanding-the-sandi:
Sandia report SAND2026-26179 documents the Sandia Message Rate benchmark and its newest extensions, by Matthew Dosanjh. The benchmark has long measured how fast a supercomputer's message layer can juggle many talks at once. Real codes swap short messages with many partners at the same time, a load that plain speed tests miss. Four set patterns drive the load: one-way flow, paired exchange, pre-posted receives, and an all-start rush. A fixed partner-picking rule keeps runs repeatable across machines.

The fresh work lets the same tests run from graphics processor memory, not just host memory. Back ends cover NVIDIA chips, AMD chips, and the Kokkos portability layer. A check mode verifies that message contents arrive intact. Sample results from the Eldorado system show how message size, placement, and partner count move the rate.
english-men-of-letters-crabbe:
Alfred Ainger tells the poet's hard life in Crabbe, his volume in the English Men of Letters series, dated 1903. Chapters move from early life in Aldeburgh through poverty in London to friendship with Burke. The parish works follow: The Parish Register, The Borough, the Tales, and Tales of the Hall.

Ainger rests chiefly on the memoir by Crabbe's son, printed in 1834, and on letters and sermons lent by the publisher John Murray. Edward FitzGerald's annotated copy of the memoir supplied anecdotes from the family. Ainger praises Crabbe's realism, a truth that could not be doubted, and his pity. The last years at Trowbridge close a life that began in a salt-marsh port and ended a country clergyman.
govdocs-archive_org-reflections-on-viole:
Georges Sorel published Reflections on Violence in 1908, and it became the key text of revolutionary syndicalism. Sorel argued that workers needed a myth to move them, above all the myth of the general strike.

By myth he meant an image of coming victory strong enough to make people act, whether or not it ever arrives as planned. The argument influenced the revolutionary left, and later the far right borrowed from it as well. Few short books on politics have traveled so far in so many directions, which is why it remains a landmark of political thought.
govdocs-archive_org-sacred-mathematics-o: Holy Numbers of the Extersteine studies the Externsteine, a line of tall sandstone rocks in Germany, through measure and number.
